newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Grenade attacks take fizz out of Hungary nightlife. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Grenade attacks take fizz out of Hungary nightlife. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT]

text.p: A spate of mystery grenade attacks near restaurants and nightclubs, which police blame on gang warfare, is taking its toll on Budapest's vibrant nightlife.

"It's putting Budapest on the map but not in a good way," said Ildiko, the manager of a striptease club which was the target of one of more than a dozen attacks this year. (Corrects to make clear that the club has been attacked only once).

Budapest, where sex clubs have flourished since the collapse of communism in 1989, was well on its way to developing a reputation as the "Bangkok of eastern Europe" before the attacks began three months ago.

Police, who believe mafia-type criminal gangs are responsible, admit they are puzzled because the owners of the targeted businesses say they have received no threats or demands for extortion payments.
"Restaurant and club owners all deny they have received any threats and that makes our job much more difficult," said Colonel Janos Lazar of the Hungarian National Police.
No one has been hurt by the attacks, which usually occur in the early hours of the morning when few patrons are around.
The explosions have damaged windows, restaurants and cars, and, in one case, destroyed a men's lavatory at one of the clubs.
Police are investigating the murder on November 1 of Jozsef Prisztas, a known underworld figure, who was shot at point-blank range with a 9mm pistol while sitting at the wheel of his jeep.

They are also trying to establish who shot and seriously wounded Csaba Lakatos, a prominent Hungarian racehorse owner. Lakatos was shot three times with a rifle as he was walked near the stables between races at Budapest's race track.
Some 1,000 people were in the stands at the time, track officials said.
Peter Szekely, the track's managing director, said Lakatos had a "strong personality" and had made enemies among the racing fraternity, but he knew of no specific link with the underworld.
"We just want police to solve these crimes," he said. "Every citizen of Budapest is getting worried."

Police announced a breakthrough last week when they said they had arrested two men as possible suspects in the attacks. An arsenal including grenades, plastic explosives and handguns was confiscated at a house used by one of them, police said.

But a day later, another grenade exploded outside a sex club in the Buda hills area, about 150 metres (490 feet) from National Police headquarters, damaging a car. Bystanders chased a man they believed had thrown the grenade but lost track of him in a nearby park.
"It is a war, it is definitely a gang war," Budapest Mayor Gabor Demszky told Reuters.
Demszky said police had thrown up a heavy security cordon around clubs, bars and restaurants and had forced criminals from nearby countries, including Ukraine and Russia, to leave.
He said Budapest was ready to increase its spending on police fivefold and called on the central government, which controls the national police, to increase its spending.
"Up to now there has been nothing very serious but naturally all this noise is very important and we have to hear this," he said.
"We have to take these signs seriously and we have to prepare ourselves for the extension of these wars which could someday include innocent civilians as targets."
A few weeks ago, the national police put 130 officers on the investigation and last week increased the force to 160.
The beefed-up security has put a definite damper on nightlife, with some regulars saying there seem to be as many police in the nightclubs as there are customers.
Nor are the club owners convinced that organised crime is to blame.
"I don't know who did it. It could just be someone who is crazy," said Ildiko, who said she had received no phone calls or letters.
"I was left with the impression that whoever did it did not want to cause real harm," she added.
But Budapest residents, particularly those who live in the city's nightlife districts, are distinctly worried.
"I only know what we hear on the radio but it must be the mafia," said a woman sweeping the pavement outside one of the targeted sex clubs and who gave her name only as Marika.

"We've never had anything like this before and it can't be just an acccident that there was a grenade outside this nightclub and not at the fruit store across the street," she said. "This is where the money is."
